items.consigne: Listen to your partner’s line. Answer the question orally with one related English sentence. Then ask one simple, relevant question.
items.stimulus: Partner says: “Our class can choose a new board game. What kind of game would you like?” The evaluator waits for the student reply and related question.
items.reponse_attendue: A model answer is: “I would like a cooperative game. Do you like working in teams?” Any coherent game type and an on-topic question are acceptable; a single unrelated answer is not.
criteres: L’élève répond en lien avec le contenu exact de l’intervention du partenaire.
Une réponse est compréhensible, sans pénalité pour l’accent non natif.
The learner asks a related question rather than giving another unrelated statement.
items.feedback: If the reply does not concern games, reread the partner’s exact question during remediation and ask what it requests. Then verify on a different prompt.

items.cible_observable: short relevant oral reply and related question; observation directe de la réponse orale et de la cohérence argumentative en contexte interactif
items.variations_permises: Game genre and question wording may vary, but the partner’s stimulus stays fixed.
contraintes_invariables: phrases du partenaire fixées comme stimulus

items.consigne: Listen to a different opinion about a fictional classroom display. Reply respectfully and ask a question that helps the conversation continue.
items.stimulus: Partner says: “I would put student drawings near the door. What would you display?”
items.reponse_attendue: One acceptable reply: “That could look welcoming. I would display our story covers. Which drawings would you choose?” Agreement is equally valid. The first idea should not ignore the partner’s drawings.
criteres: Student shows by wording or relevant response that the partner proposed drawings.
Student gives a clearly related idea or response.
Student asks a useful on-topic question.
Message is intelligible independent of accent.
items.feedback: If the student only announces an opinion, model a brief acknowledgement after the attempt, then check with a new partner claim.

items.consigne: In spoken English, state one choice and a reason that explains how it meets the fictional group’s goal.
items.stimulus: Situation: The fictional class wants a quiet activity while other groups read. Choices: puzzles or sketching. Partner asks: “What would you suggest, and why?”
items.reponse_attendue: A sound answer: “I suggest sketching because students can work quietly while readers concentrate.” Equally acceptable: “I suggest puzzles because small groups can solve them quietly.” “Because it is better” alone is insufficient.
criteres: Choice addresses the quiet-activity situation.
Reason identifies a concrete advantage relevant to quiet study.
Choice and reason are orally linked and intelligible.
items.feedback: If the learner offers only a preference, ask after the attempt what benefit it provides to quiet readers; train then retest on a different context.

items.consigne: Present your idea and explain it with both a reason and a specific example spoken aloud.
items.stimulus: Fictional context: A school can set up a small shared reading table. Partner asks: “Would a reading table help?”
items.reponse_attendue: A coherent answer: “Yes. It could help students share books because they would have a place to read together. For example, two pupils could take turns reading a short story at the table.” An alternative valid answer may reject the table with a reason and illustrative situation.
criteres: Idea is explicitly accepted or rejected.
Reason explains a consequence linked to a shared reading table.
Example names a plausible specific action, participant, place or occasion.
English message is understandable without demanding flawless grammar.
items.feedback: If the example just says “It helps”, ask for one imagined action that makes the benefit visible; practise with a different proposal.

items.consigne: During a live exchange, ask for clarification, listen to the reply and answer appropriately; then tell the listener why your choice fits.
items.stimulus: Partner first asks softly: “Where could we display the new posters?” After a learner clarification request, the partner repeats exactly: “Where could we display the new posters?” The room has a door and a blank display board.
items.reponse_attendue: Accept: “Could you repeat the question, please?” → after repetition: “On the display board, because students can see them there.” A direct relevant answer is also acceptable if the question was heard. Requesting repetition is not penalized.
criteres: Student detects or resolves message uncertainty appropriately.
Final response supplies a plausible location from the scenario.
Reason relates location to visibility or access.
Turn-taking remains courteous and intelligible.
items.feedback: If the student guesses unrelated content, pause after the attempt, show a supported repair phrase and test a fresh question.

items.consigne: Participate in four alternating turns, including one question to your partner. Then present your choice, a reason and an example in English.
items.stimulus: Partner turn 1: “Should our fictional class start a puzzle club?” Learner turn 2 must answer and ask a related question. Partner turn 3: “I might prefer a drawing club. How could your club include beginners?” Learner turn 4 responds. Then the student presents.
items.reponse_attendue: One complete possible dialogue: “Yes, puzzles encourage teamwork. Which club would you choose?” / “Beginners could work with partners, so no one has to solve a puzzle alone.” Presentation: “I recommend a puzzle club because students can practise solving problems together. For example, two beginners could share an easy puzzle.” A justified drawing club is also permitted.
criteres: Actual exchange has alternating A–student–A–student turns.
Student both answers partner prompts and asks a connected question.
Short presentation has a claim, relevant reason and concrete example.
English remains understandable despite small errors or accent variation.
items.feedback: If the student only recites a paragraph, rehearse response to a partner’s changed question; if presentation lacks example, ask for who-does-what detail.

items.consigne: Respond to a different view, ask a follow-up and then offer a short reasoned presentation of your proposal.
items.stimulus: Partner: “I think a storytelling wall would take too much space. What do you think?” Learner responds and asks one on-topic question. Partner follows up: “We only have a narrow display board. How could we make it smaller?” Learner answers and then presents.
items.reponse_attendue: Example: “We could use only one section of the wall. How much space is available?” / “We could choose six short stories on the narrow board and replace them every month.” Presentation: “I support a small storytelling wall because it would let pupils share writing. For example, six stories could fit on a narrow display board.” A well-reasoned alternative is accepted.
criteres: Learner acknowledges the space concern instead of ignoring it.
A relevant question enables an actual partner response.
Reply addresses the second partner question about size.
Mini-presentation includes an argued idea and concrete example.
items.feedback: If the space concern disappears from the reply, replay the partner’s objection in a teaching setting; then retry with a new scenario.

items.consigne: Talk with a museum-guide partner about making a display easier for visitors; then present your proposal with a reason and a specific example.
items.stimulus: Partner says: “Visitors often miss our small exhibit. What should we change?” Student answers and asks a question. Partner says: “That sounds useful. Would your change help younger visitors too?” Student responds and then presents.
items.reponse_attendue: For example: “We could add a bright, clearly labelled sign. Would a picture help?” / “Yes. A sign with a large picture could guide younger visitors.” Presentation: “I suggest a clear sign because visitors need to find the exhibit easily. For example, a sign with a dinosaur picture could point towards the dinosaur models.” Another justified change may pass.
criteres: Student makes a relevant improvement proposal and asks a genuine question.
Student explicitly responds to the follow-up about younger visitors.
Presentation has a clear idea, a supporting reason and a situation-based example.
Observer records two-way exchange and intelligibility.
items.feedback: If learner only talks about signs with no reply to the younger-visitors question, practise listening to the question then retest in another fixed venue.

items.consigne: INDEPENDENT ASSESSMENT A. Use a fictional plan for Community Reading Day. Have a real four-turn exchange with a partner, then present your idea, reason and example in English. The partner’s exact lines are provided; do not receive language or content hints during the attempt.
items.stimulus: Fixed scenario: The event can host EITHER a storytelling circle OR a book-swap table. Goal: help visitors enjoy reading. Partner turn 1: “Which activity would you choose for Community Reading Day?” Student turn 2: answer and ask a relevant question. Partner turn 3: “I like the storytelling circle. How would your choice welcome new visitors?” Student turn 4: reply to that point. Then learner gives a short separate oral mini-presentation. Evaluator writes observation notes; no recording needed.
items.reponse_attendue: One model, NOT to be read to the learner: “I suggest a book-swap table. Which activity would you choose?” / “A book swap could welcome newcomers because they could discover books without bringing their own. We could provide a few starter books.” Then: “I recommend a book-swap table because it lets visitors discover different stories. For example, someone could choose a book from the starter shelf and share a recommendation.” Storytelling-circle answers are equally valid if reasoned. Evaluator records whether partner’s words were answered and an actual question was asked.
criteres: M1: Learner answers both fixed partner questions contingently, with accurate uptake of their meanings.
M2: Learner yields a turn, asks at least one relevant question, and sustains a genuine four-turn exchange.
M3: Mini-presentation states a comprehensible choice and a relevant explanatory reason.
M4: Mini-presentation provides one specific plausible example supporting that reason.
M5: English is intelligible and both parts are produced without directive lexical/content help during assessment (agreed nondirective access supports allowed).
items.feedback: Missing M1/M2: targeted listening and turn-taking practice; missing M3: compare cause to circular reason; missing M4: require a concrete who/what/where example in a new task; M5: adjust access and obtain human equivalence review when needed. Never grade accent identity.
items.representation: production orale interactive observée avec partenaire; mini-présentation orale lorsque spécifiée; trace écrite par évaluateur
items.cible_observable: autonomous mastery observation A; separate from scenario B; observation directe de la réponse orale et de la cohérence argumentative en contexte interactif
items.variations_permises: Choices of the TWO specified activities, fictional details of illustration, pace and pre-agreed nonleading accommodations may vary. Partner dialogue, 4-turn requirement and idea-reason-example structure may not vary.
contraintes_invariables: phrases du partenaire fixées comme stimulus

items.consigne: INDEPENDENT ASSESSMENT B. In a different fictional context, discuss a garden-day proposal with a partner and then independently present your proposal with a reason and concrete example. Create a fresh idea; do not merely repeat the Reading Day speech.
items.stimulus: Fixed scenario: A school will hold a Garden Day and can choose EITHER a seed-label workshop OR a garden-observation walk. Goal: help visitors learn about plants. Partner turn 1: “What should visitors do during School Garden Day?” Student turn 2: answer and ask one relevant follow-up. Partner turn 3: “I would choose the garden-observation walk. What could visitors learn from your activity?” Student turn 4: respond to the exact question, acknowledging the partner’s activity as appropriate. Then deliver a distinct oral mini-presentation, without prompts.
items.reponse_attendue: One model, NOT to be given during assessment: “I suggest the seed-label workshop. Which activity would you choose?” / “They could learn the names of plants and where the seeds belong. A walk would also help them look closely at plants.” Then: “I recommend a seed-label workshop because clear labels can help visitors identify plants. For example, learners could label three seed trays with plant names.” Observation-walk proposals are equally correct if supported. A reasonable fictional example is accepted; do not require specialist botany knowledge.
criteres: M1: Learner answers both fixed partner questions contingently, with accurate uptake of their meanings.
M2: Learner yields a turn, asks at least one relevant question, and sustains a genuine four-turn exchange.
M3: Mini-presentation states a comprehensible choice and a relevant explanatory reason.
M4: Mini-presentation provides one specific plausible example supporting that reason.
M5: English is intelligible and both parts are produced without directive lexical/content help during assessment (agreed nondirective access supports allowed).
items.feedback: Use a fresh nonleading garden task to remediate missing responsive turn-taking, idea-reason link or concrete example. Do not award mastery on a memorized second reading speech. Accommodation decisions remain individualized and reviewed by a human.
items.representation: production orale interactive observée avec partenaire; mini-présentation orale lorsque spécifiée; trace écrite par évaluateur
items.cible_observable: autonomous mastery observation B, different setting and new idea; observation directe de la réponse orale et de la cohérence argumentative en contexte interactif
items.variations_permises: Choose from the TWO specified garden activities and supply original coherent details. Partner prompts and assessment dimensions fixed; physical setting, pace and approved access supports may vary.
